# Researchers put the air we breathe through the filter of science

**That is one of the objectives of the 4DAir program, developed by the EAFIT, del Valle, Nacional and La Salle universities, with funding from MinCiencias, which seeks to broadly understand air pollution in Medellín, Bogotá and Cali.**

**This project has created instruments to measure air pollution and determine the composition of particulate matter in the air. The proposal aims to understand how pollutants move and to make more accurate forecasts.**

- [Start](https://www.eafit.edu.co/)
- [News](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias)
- [Our Impact](https://www.eafit.edu.co/noticias/nuestro-impacto)
- Researchers put the air we breathe through the filter of science

![Imagen Investigadores pasan el aire que respiramos por el filtro de la ciencia](https://universidadeafit.widen.net/content/8e94b6c7-d896-4c94-acb0-2469006b6e1c/web/el-aire-que-respiramos.jpg?crop=yes&k=c&w=823&h=450&itok=3GctiCW_)

The Lidar system, developed at EAFIT, is a radar that uses laser light to remotely measure the concentration of polluting particles in the atmosphere.

Air quality once again takes center stage in March, when a combination of atmospheric events prevents pollution from escaping the Aburrá Valley. With the aim of finding solutions to this problem affecting various urban centers across the country, and to provide scientific evidence for decision-making, the 4DAir program was launched. This initiative, funded by MinCiencias, involves the universities EAFIT, del Valle, Nacional, and La Salle.

_Estimation of urban pollution through the use of measurements and assimilation of surface, in situ and remote sensing data_ (4DAir-MOLIS) is the name of this proposal, which seeks to offer relevant information from three research projects focused on: development of measurement instruments; morphological and chemical characterization of particulate matter, and analysis of mathematical models of meteorology.

According to Elena Montilla Rosero, director of the program and professor at the School of Applied Sciences and Engineering of EAFIT, the first project has created instruments for measuring particulate matter and gases in the atmosphere in two formats: in situ, located at surface level, and remote detection, capable of covering large volumes of information, such as the Lidar system, which uses laser light to measure from one hundred meters above surface level, with the great advantage of being able to move the laser in different directions.

Both instruments bear the University's hallmark, as the _on-site_ microstations were developed with the support of EAFIT _spin-off_ SimpleSpace , while the Lidar system was the product of the work of Manuela Hoyos Restrepo, an EAFIT graduate and doctoral student at the French Space Agency, and Professor Elena. Since last year, they have been able to use the instruments in measurement campaigns in Bogotá, Cali, and Medellín, seeking to understand, among other questions, where pollution goes during times that are not normally analyzed.

“For now, we are looking at the entire volume of air within the Aburrá Valley to understand broadly where the pollution is coming from and where it is moving, because it is not only how the Valley is affected, but also how the surrounding ecosystems and their biodiversity are affected,” says the program director, adding that with this information, more relevant measures can be taken and the data currently presented by the Early Warning System network of Medellín and the Aburrá Valley (Siata) can be complemented.

Of this first project, it is important to highlight the recent collaboration between EAFIT and the University of Valle for the development of a remote detection system called DOAS, which is expected to provide relevant information for the measurement of polluting gases, such as nitrogen dioxide.

The second project aimed to determine the composition of particulate matter. To achieve this, an intelligent system was designed to establish the chemical and morphological composition of polluting particles, a process that was previously costly. Knowing this information will allow for the identification of sources and the focusing of efforts on mitigating certain types of activities in the short and medium term.

Finally, the third project focuses on mathematical models to describe atmospheric processes, determine their sources, and predict their behavior: “We managed to couple a meteorological model with chemical models,” says Olga Lucía Quintero Montoya, a researcher and professor at the School of Applied Sciences and Engineering at EAFIT, who has also participated in this program. She also emphasizes that incorporating the measurements from the first project will improve the capabilities of these models.

The 4DAir program will soon present the results of its analyses; however, they emphasize that this initiative has generated a technologically independent working methodology, which complements the results of the _Exposure to Pollutants Regional Research_ (ExPoR2) program very well. This program identified the adverse health effects of exposure to particulate matter in the air of the Aburrá Valley and led to the _spin-off_ Bottom, dedicated to manufacturing nanofiber filters for masks and industries.

Engaging in dialogue with decision-makers and air quality specialists is one of the program team's next challenges. Professor Elena concludes that one of their goals is "to present the tools we've developed and are making available to the community and relevant authorities so that we can work together on future projects with these new tools, which until now weren't readily available in Medellín and Cali, or even in Bogotá."

###### Living intelligently

While industrial emissions contribute significantly to poor air quality, they are already regulated, whereas vehicle emissions require even more intervention. Professor Olga Lucía argues, based on previous studies she has conducted, that having a road network free of traffic congestion is one of the best ways to regulate emissions of polluting gases.

To achieve this, he explains, an exclusive lane on the right would have to be maintained for buses: “If there is a dedicated lane for public transport, traffic jams are reduced by 80%.” Light vehicles would travel on the left at high speed, while the central lanes would be used for overtaking in some cases or for motorcycle traffic, in order to maintain a consistent speed on the roads and reduce congestion.

With certain measures, vehicle emission profiles could be regulated during the day, allowing the atmosphere to do its job of dispersing pollutants: “We can’t control the wind, but we can live intelligently,” says the researcher, highlighting that carpooling or implementing peak-hour traffic restrictions are good practices that could be complemented by measures to control traffic flow, density, and speed.

###### Viruses versus bacteria: PhageLife's proposal for the swine sector from EAFIT

En una granja porcina, una infección bacteriana puede poner en riesgo la salud de los animales y la productividad del negocio. Además, el problema se vuelve más complejo cuando las bacterias dejan de responder a los antibióticos que antes permitían combatirlas. Para explorar otra vía, la empresa [PhageLife](https://phagelife.co/) desarrolla soluciones personalizadas con bacteriófagos, virus naturales capaces de eliminar bacterias específicas.

metadata.ogTitle: Investigadores pasan el aire que respiramos por el filtro de la ciencia
metadata.ogDescription: La calidad del aire vuelve a ser el centro de atención en marzo, cuando la conjunción de eventos atmosféricos impide que la contaminación salga del Valle de Aburrá. Con la intención de encontrar soluciones a esta problemática que aqueja a distintos centros urbanos del país, y de ofrecer evidencia científica para la toma de decisiones, surgió el programa 4DAir, una iniciativa financiada por MinCiencias en la que participan las universidades EAFIT, del Valle, Nacional y La Salle.
